## Summary Scores

-   **Sensitivity:** High
-   **Exposure:** Moderate
-   **Vulnerability:** Moderate

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Define the directory and the correct file extension pattern
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "\\.pdf$", "\\.png$")
dir_path <- here::here("figures/Witch flounder")

# Search for any file containing the string AND the correct extension
found_files <- list.files(
  path = dir_path, 
  pattern = paste0("combined_table_allvars.*", ext), 
  full.names = TRUE
)

has_figure <- length(found_files) > 0

if (has_figure) {
  # Get metadata for all matching files
  file_details <- file.info(found_files)
  
  # Find the row with the maximum (newest) modification time
  newest_index <- which.max(file_details$mtime)
  
  # Assign the newest file's path to img_path
  img_path <- found_files[newest_index]
} else {
  img_path <- NULL
}
```


## Score Descriptions:

### Sensitivity:

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Define the directory and the correct file extension pattern
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "\\.pdf$", "\\.png$")
dir_path <- here::here("figures/Witch flounder")

# Search for any file containing the string AND the correct extension
found_files <- list.files(
  path = dir_path, 
  pattern = paste0("sensitivity.*", ext), 
  full.names = TRUE
)

has_figure <- length(found_files) > 0

if (has_figure) {
  # Get metadata for all matching files
  file_details <- file.info(found_files)
  
  # Find the row with the maximum (newest) modification time
  newest_index <- which.max(file_details$mtime)
  
  # Assign the newest file's path to img_path
  img_path <- found_files[newest_index]
} else {
  img_path <- NULL
}

# Store the TRUE/FALSE result 
has_figure <- file.exists(img_path)
```

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| fig-cap: "Witch flounder Sensitivity on the Northeast Shelf"
#| label: fig-sens-witchfl
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"

knitr::include_graphics(img_path)
```

Witch flounder received a **High** sensitivity score, with 100% certainty. Two attributes had scores greater than 3: Stock Size (3.9) and Population Growth Rate (3.5) (@fig-sum-tab-witchfl).

Winter flounder are a long-lived, slowly maturing species, reaching maturity at 4.5-6 years and living up to 30 year [@burnett1992several] [@cargnelli1999_witch]. The stock status is poorly understood; the stock is overfished but it is unclear if overfishing is occurring due to lack of data [@nefsc2024witch].

Witch flounder also received a High sensitivity score in the 2016 Climate Vulnerability Assessment. This was also driven by Stock Size and Population Growth Rate [@hare2016vulnerability].

Mean exposure for Witch flounder was **Moderate** (1.98 +/- 0.93) (@fig-sum-tab-witchfl). Exposure was Very High over Georges Bank and High in southern New England, along the coast of the Gulf of Maine, and along the continental shelf break (@fig-exp-witchfl). These patterns were driven by bottom temperature, oxygen, and aragonite solubility exposures (@fig-fact-exp-witchfl).

In the previous Assessment, witch flounder received a High Exposure score, driven by sea surface temperature and ocean acidification [@hare2016vulnerability].

Mean Vulnerability for Witch flounder was **Moderate** (5.93 +/- 2.80) (@fig-sum-tab-witchfl). Vulnerability was Very High over Georges Bank and High in Southern New England, along the coast of the Gulf of Maine, and on the shelf break (@fig-vuln-witchfl). 

In the previous assessment, Witch flounder received a High Vulnerability score [@hare2016vulnerability].

## Data Quality Metrics

### Life History Data Quality:

78% of data quality scores were greater than or equal to 2, indicating good data quality. Both Adult Mobility and Egg and Larval Survival and Settlement Requirements were identified as data gaps (mean attribute data quality score \< 2) (@fig-sum-tab-witchfl).

### Model Confidence Score:

Mean model confidence was 2.1 (+/- 0.4) indicating moderate confidence in the models. Experts stated that predicted distributions met expectations, but the model tended to under-predict species presence in the Gulf of Maine. The ensemble AUC score was 0.91, indicating excellent prediction accuracy.

Circles represent points from the MOM6 hindcast; triangles represent points from the MOM6 forecast. Dashed lines represent significant linear regressions"

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
*Note: For an animated version of this plot, please see the online version of this document.*
:::

Witch flounder experienced significant core habitat and range loss between 1993 and 2023. Core habitat losses occurred on the continental shelf break and throughout the Gulf of Maine. Winter flounder lost range along the continental shelf, with the range contracting towards the shelfbreak and away from the coast in the Mid Atlantic Bight (@fig-shifts-witchfl). The weighted centroid shifted 39 km northeast. 

Under near-future ocean conditions, winter flounder core habitat and range is expected to expand. Witch flounder are predicted to gain habitat in the Gulf of Maine. Their range is expected to expand westward on the continental shelf towards the coast in the Gulf of Maine (@fig-shifts-witchfl). The weighted centroid is predicted to shift 5 km south. 

In the previous Assessment, witch flounder received a High Distributional Vulnerability Rank [@hare2016vulnerability]. 

| Time Period | Weighted Centroid Shift (km & bearing) | Core Habitat Area (change) (km^2^) | Habitat Total Area (change) (km^2^) | Latitude Range (change) (deg) | Change in Longitude Range (deg) |
|------------|------------|------------|------------|------------|------------|
| 1993-1997 | NA | 57,399  | 192,655 | 4.99 | 6.65 |
| 2019-2023 | 39.0 km NE | 49,226 (-8,172) | 182,690 (-9,965) | 4.36 (-0.62) | 5.85 (-0.80) |
| 2031-2035 | 5.1 km S | 51,306 (+2,079) | 185,858 (+3,169) | 4.55 (+0.19) | 6.17 (+0.32) |

### Directional Effect:

Experts predicted that witch flounder will be **negatively** impacted by climate change, with certainty equal to 95%. This is similar, but with higher certainty, to the 2016 Climate Vulnerability Assessment, which also predicted negative impacts from climate change on witch flounder [@hare2016vulnerability]. While there are few direct studies of the impacts of climate change on witch flounder, adults are known to prefer relatively cold temperatures between 4-11 C [@cargnelli1999_witch]. A recent study suggests that distributions are shifting southward [@mills2024multispecies].

## Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution

There have been few direct studies on the effect of climate change on witch flounder. Larval growth and survival has been linked to temperature in laboratory conditions [@bidwell2001effect]. @murawski1993climate included witch flounder in a list of species that exhibit low variation in seasonal temperature or depth of occurrence. @mills2024multispecies found that witch flounder distribution has actually shifted significantly toward more southern latitudes.

## Life History Synopsis

Witch flounder are a long-lived flatfish species inhabiting deep, cold waters in the Northwest Atlantic from Labrador to North Carolina [@cargnelli1999_witch]. They are slow-growing, reaching maturity at 4.5 years for males and 6 years for females in Georges Bank and the Gulf of Maine [@burnett1992several]. Witch flounder can live up to 30 years, reaching a maximum length of 78 cm [@cargnelli1999_witch]. Witch flounder spawn from March to November, with peak spawning occurring in summer. The general trend is for spawning to occur progressively later from south to north. In the Gulf of Maine-Georges Bank region, spawning occurs from April to November, and peaks from May to August [@martin1978development] [@burnett1992several]. @powles1970depth suggested that witch flounder occupy three largely discrete ecological niches, resulting in the different life stages being geographically separated from each other. The pelagic egg and larval stages are spent in the water column over deep water. Egg hatching occurs 7 to 8 days after spawning, with the yolk sac absorbed 10 days after hatching. Larvae are pelagic, and the larval stage lasts from 4-6 months to 1 year [@cargnelli1999_witch]. Eggs generally drift southward, and shelf currents may transport some larvae. Length may be the biggest cue for settlement [@cargnelli1999_witch]. The juvenile stage occurs in very deep water when metamorphosed fish settle to the bottom. They are found over mud, clay, silt, or muddy sand substrates [@cargnelli1999_witch]. Juveniles remain separated from the adult population, occupying deeper areas until the onset of sexual maturity. @walsh1987habitat suggests however that while the juveniles and adults are in different areas, the niche separation may not be true. Witch flounder are capable of inhabiting depths up to 1500 m, although the majority are found at 90-300 m [@martin1978development] [@kleinmacphee2002witch]. The main food items in the witch flounder diet are polychaetes and crustaceans, although mollusks and echinoderms are also important. Overall, polychaetes were by far the most important food item, accounting for greater than 70% of the diet [@maurer1975food]. However, there is a distinct ontogenetic shift in diet, with polychaetes increasing in importance and crustaceans decreasing in importance with age [@cargnelli1999_witch]. Adult witch flounder generally do not migrate, although they prefer to stay within temperatures of 4-11°C. Some subpopulations may move from shallower waters in warmer months to deeper overwintering waters. Migration was not observed in the Gulf of Maine [@cargnelli1999_witch]. Predators of witch flounder include monkfish, spiny dogfish, harp seals, Atlantic halibut, white hake, and some skates [@kleinmacphee2002witch]. Witch flounder are managed as a single stock unit by the New England Fishery Management Council under the Northeast Multispecies (Groundfish) Fishery Management Plan. In the last Management Track Assessment, the stock status could not be determined due to a lack of biological reference points. The stock condition appears to be improving but is poor relative to historical levels [@nefsc2024witch].

Exposure oscillated between Low and Moderate on average across months. Exposure was Moderate in January, March - April, and July - September (@fig-exp-month-witchfl). These patterns were driven by coincident peaks in bottom temperature, oxygen, and salinity as well as downward particulate organic carbon flux (@fig-exp-month-tm-witchfl).

Bottom temperature, salinity, and aragonite solubility were important dynamic drivers of witch flounder distributions (@fig-radar-witchfl). Witch flounder occupy cold, deep waters [@cargnelli1999_witch]. Diets are dominated by polychaetes but mollusks and echinoderms also play important roles [@maurer1975food]. When only these factors were used to calculate exposure, mean exposure decreased to Low (1.48 +/- 0.79) (@fig-sum-imp-witchfl; @fig-exp-imp-witchfl).

```{r}
  img_path <- NULL
}
```
